newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish economy in EMU dilemma - it is doing too well.
newsitem.headline: Irish economy in EMU dilemma - it is doing too well.

text.p: As the race to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) hots up, the Irish government is faced with a singular dilemma -- its economy is doing too well.

While other EU governments are accused of manipulating their accounts to enhance their chances of qualifying, the Irish government must hold back from stimulating economic growth too much in case it creates unwanted inflationary pressure. "We are unique in Europe in that all our problems are to do with overheating rather than problems to do with under-performing," Dan McLaughlin, economist with Riada stockbrokers, told Reuters.

Such is the robustness of the Irish economy that official data on Wednesday showed the exchequer running a cumulative surplus of 185 million punts to end-September, the first time in decades the government's coffers have been in the black.

Ireland's 1997 budget deficit, forecast at about 2.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), is comfortably within the 3.0-percent target laid down under the EU's Maastricht treaty requirements to qualify for EMU.
But Maastricht's requirement that inflation must not be more than 1.5-percent higher than the three best performing states is a little more worrying for the Dublin authorities.
The staunchly pro-EU government vowed to be among the first wave of EMU qualifiers. But 1997 is not only the year that will determine who is "in" and who is "out" of EMU.
It is also an election year for Prime Minister John Bruton's "rainbow coalition" government, grouping his centre-right Fine Gael party, the Labour party and the radical Democratic Left.
The coalition is already under pressure in opinion polls, which show Bruton and Labour party deputy Dick Spring both losing ground in the popularity stakes.
With money in the coffers, a giveaway January budget involving much sought-after tax cuts followed swiftly by a general election is just too tempting, economists said.

"Given the state of the public finances now the scope for significant tax cuts ahead of an election budget will be probably be too difficult for the Minister of Finance to resist," economist Oliver Mangan of Davy Stockbrokers said.
Such a budget might win votes but stimulate growth to the point that inflation may rise to the outer limits or even beyond the Maastricht requirement, economists said.
"It would be ironic if Ireland failed to qualify for EMU after years of being comfortably within the Maastricht criteria," Riada's McLaughlin said.

Ireland's inflation level in the first half of 1996 was a comfortable 1.5 percent. Bloxham stockbrokers economist Alan McQuaid expects this to move up to 2.5 percent in 1997, which may trigger alarm bells. McQuaid estimates the current EU inflation average at 1.1 to 1.3 percent.

Credit growth data from the central bank on Thursday is expected to confirm a stubbornly high growth rate of more than 14 percent while mortgage lending is expected to hover around 15 percent or more.

Economists believe the central bank will be far from happy with such strong growth, but its hands are tied as it tries to balance the Irish currency against its European counterparts while containing interest rates and inflationary pressures.
"The bottom line is that the central bank will continually try and keep interest rates firm. The last thing the central bank wants is to stimulate growth any more," an economist said.
